summary: This work develops a theory for readout-induced transmon lifetime degradation by incorporating drive-renormalized qubit spectral shapes beyond the weak-coupling limit, showing that the qubit emission spectrum becomes non-Lorentzian and depends sensitively on readout drive frequency even at fixed measurement rate. Experiments on a strongly dispersive transmon ($|\chi|/\kappa = 1$ to $4$) validate the predictions quantitatively and reveal that driving at the ground-state resonator frequency $\omega_r^{(g)}$ minimizes $T_1$ degradation by producing the narrowest emission spectrum.
motivation: Dispersive readout of superconducting qubits degrades with increasing drive power due to enhanced qubit-TLS interaction, but existing Lorentzian broadening models fail in modern devices operating at large $|\chi|/\kappa$ ratios where spectral reshaping becomes non-trivial.
method: The authors generalize number-splitting theory to derive the qubit decay rate via Fermi's golden rule applied to the drive-modified emission spectrum, incorporating state-dependent resonator loss rates from Purcell filters. Theory is validated against master equation simulations and experiments on a flux-tunable transmon coupled to a Purcell-filtered resonator with $\chi/2\pi = -8.8$ MHz and $\kappa_g/2\pi = 9.0$ MHz.
result: For a fixed measurement rate, driving at $\omega_d = \omega_r^{(g)}$ yields narrower qubit spectra and substantially less $T_1$ degradation than driving at $\omega_d = \omega_r^{(e)}$ (separated by $\chi$), with quantitative agreement between theory and measurements on both far-detuned ($\Delta_{\mathrm{tls}}/2\pi \approx -16$ MHz) and near-resonant ($\Delta_{\mathrm{tls}}/2\pi \approx -6$ MHz) TLSs.
